endorsements.quote: Training healthcare professionals in recognizing failure modes and offering a simple mechanism to disable autonomous AI when necessary is essential to avoid unchecked errors that could jeopardize patient care.
The capacity to disable the AI system swiftly and effectively in the event of failure is crucial for patient safety.

Stakeholders in implementation of AI tools in clinical practice should therefore familiarize themselves with the relevant methods and metrics for clinical evaluation and devise strategies to verify performance claims prior to tool introduction, and should continuously monitor performance during routine usage [ 64 ].

Therefore, as the use of AI becomes more prevalent and the AI tools being deployed become more diverse, institutions using AI should establish ongoing performance oversight as one function of a local AI governance process [ 78 ].

Institutions should develop a clearly defined escalation and resolution strategy when monitoring detects model failure or performance drift occurs that defines the notification and action plan, and the mode of operation while the model performance is being assessed and the cause of model failure determined.
This process should be repeated whenever relevant changes are made to the AI software or the equipment used in combination with the AI.

Of course, vendors will have performed testing and quality assurance of the respective AI tools during regulatory approval, but purchasers should consider validation of the AI\u2019s performance on a local dataset, and adjust parameters if needed prior to implementation in clinical practice.
The concept of transparency should also extend to patients being made aware if AI systems are being used.

For any AI tool to be successfully integrated into clinical practice, stakeholders should first clearly identify areas that need improvement and define relevant key performance indicators [ 52 , 53 ].
Return on investment (RoI) and cost\u2013benefit analyses should be planned and carried out to ensure the viability of the planned AI integration.

Finally, continuous user education throughout the lifecycle of AI utilization and monitoring radiologist AI usage and the combined accuracy of radiologist plus AI are instrumental in ensuring optimal patient care.
Autonomous AI should be designed to initiate actions that are transparent, identifiable, and discoverable.

unlisted_practices: Regulators should require developers to report a range of expected performance and specific failure conditions and errors rather than a single summary accuracy figure.
Regulators should encourage developers to publish model or system cards analyzing limitations, errors, and biases.
Regulatory models should distinguish advisory, semi-automated, and automated systems, requiring a deeper evidence base and real-world track record for greater autonomy.
Regulators should require an explicit post-market quality assurance plan from AI developers.
Developers should involve clinicians early in the design and development of AI tools and target unmet clinical needs.

Developers should require higher standards of empirical evidence, including external or multi-centre test data and prospective real-world evaluation, when model transparency and explainability are poor.
Vendors should establish a clear error-reporting procedure with named responsible contacts that is easily accessible to clinical end users.
Health systems should evaluate AI performance on local data using radiologist-facing metrics such as PPV and NPV and categorize false positives and false negatives to set user expectations.
Health systems should integrate AI tools into existing clinical workflows so users need not switch between applications.
Health systems should allow radiologists to modify AI results in PACS and feed the corrections back to the AI vendor.
Health systems should assess the detectability, correctability, and impact of anticipated AI errors in addition to error frequency.
Health systems should use input-distribution checks and comparison across multiple AI models for earlier insight into autonomous AI accuracy.
Health systems should monitor changes in input metadata such as equipment, protocols, and demographics.
Health systems should use a control sample of held-out difficult cases to detect performance deviations.

screen.reason: Multi-society consensus statement/framework providing practical considerations and recommendations for developing, purchasing, implementing, and monitoring AI tools in radiology.
